concept.name: Log return
concept.definition: The natural logarithm of the gross return (price ratio) over a period, equivalent to the continuously compounded rate of return. Its key property is time-additivity: multi-period log returns are the sum of single-period log returns.
concept.intuition: Log returns convert compounding into addition. Gains and losses become symmetric: +10% and -10% log returns cancel exactly to zero, unlike simple returns.
concept.mechanics: Take the natural log of the ratio of final to initial value. Because log returns add across periods, they are preferred for statistical modeling, aggregation over time, and continuous-time finance; they approximate simple returns closely when the period change is small.
concept.formula: r_t = ln(V_t / V_{t-1}) = ln(1 + R_t), where V_t and V_{t-1} are the final and initial values and R_t is the simple return. Multi-period: r_{1..T} = SUM r_t = ln(V_T / V_0).
concept.failure_modes: Log returns are undefined for a final value of zero or negative and diverge to minus infinity as value approaches zero, so they behave badly for instruments that can hit zero. Portfolio-level log returns are not the weighted sum of asset log returns (that property holds only for simple returns), so they must be converted back before portfolio aggregation.
concept.misconceptions: Log returns are not identical to simple returns except approximately for small changes: +50% simple corresponds to 40.55% log, and -50% simple to -69.31% log. Treating a mean log return as an arithmetic mean return understates or overstates expected growth if conversion is skipped.
concept.example: A stock closes at $3.570 one day and $3.575 the next; the daily log return is ln(3.575/3.570) = 0.0014, or 0.14%.
